title: The hundred are full
hook: Shishupala challenges Krishna to fight, and Krishna finally speaks: the pardons are used up
carry: kshama has a limit: dharma must be protected

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma told of Shishupala's birth and Krishna's hundred pardons. Kshama: forbearance is a godly quality.

Bhishma's story should have cooled the room. It does the opposite. Shishupala hears that he's been spared all his life by Krishna's promise, and he isn't grateful. He's insulted. He turns from Bhishma to Krishna himself and calls him out: stand up and fight me. For the first time in this whole scene, the challenge is aimed straight at the silent guest, with every king watching. And after all that waiting, Krishna speaks.
screen: `THE STORY DOESN'T COOL HIM.` → `FIGHT ME.` → `THE SILENT GUEST STANDS.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't answer Shishupala first. He turns to the kings. In the telling, he lays out what Shishupala has done: wrongs against Krishna's own people, some of them while Krishna was far away and couldn't defend them. He reminds the hall that Shishupala is his aunt's son, and that for her sake he has borne all of it. Then comes the line the whole week has waited for, in effect: the hundred are full. The promise has been kept to the end. Shishupala doesn't back down. He laughs at Krishna and dares him to do his worst. So Krishna calls to mind his discus, the spinning weapon that is his in the stories, and it comes to his hand. In front of all the kings, he strikes, and the king of Chedi falls. The order matters. Krishna doesn't strike at the first insult, or the tenth, or when Bhima wants to. He waits until his word has been fully kept, and even then he explains himself first. Here's the Hindu teaching underneath. Later in this same epic, in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says why he comes into the world at all: whenever dharma, the right order of things, declines and wrong rises, he comes, to protect the good, to end wrongdoing, and to set dharma back on its feet. So kshama and the discus aren't opposites. Both serve dharma. Mercy runs long, a hundred pardons long, but it never becomes permission for wrong to win. Some readers find the ending hard; some find it just. The poem lets us hold both.
screen: `KRISHNA SPEAKS TO THE KINGS.` · `THE HUNDRED ARE FULL.` · `THE DISCUS, ONCE HIS WORD IS KEPT.` · `GITA 4: TO PROTECT DHARMA.` · then, large: `KSHAMA HAS A LIMIT: DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind somewhere you've been patient a long time, with a person or with a habit of your own. Ask the dharma question, not the anger question: is my patience still protecting what's good, or is it letting a wrong grow? You don't have to decide now; breathe in steadiness, and breathe out the strain of waiting. If you pray, ask for clear sight about it; if not, rest with the question.
Shishupala. The king who challenged Krishna once too often, after a hundred pardons kept for his mother's sake had run out.
Your line: kshama has a limit: dharma must be protected. Krishna's was set long before the hall. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 762 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LIGHT THAT ENTERED KRISHNA.`

howItsDone: In the Bhagavad Gita (4.7–8), Krishna says he comes whenever dharma declines, to protect the good, end wrongdoing and re-establish dharma. In Hindu retellings and devotional art, the Sudarshana discus is one of Krishna's signs, and some tellers present the end of Shishupala as the moment his long patience reaches its promised limit.

original.note: Sanskrit cakra: wheel or discus; Krishna's discus comes to his hand at the end of the scene.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that Krishna addresses the kings and lists Shishupala's past wrongs against the Yadavas, some committed while Krishna was away; the specific wrongs are deliberately not named.
Confirm Krishna says, in sense, that the pardons promised to his aunt are now exhausted, and that Shishupala laughs and taunts him.
Confirm the discus comes to Krishna's hand when he thinks of it.
The death is described briefly and without gore on purpose.
